name: Kingside attacks
summary: How attacks on a castled king are built, how they are stopped, and the positions to practise them on — every one a real game from the 46th Olympiad with the engine's answer already confirmed.

patterns.name: The sacrifice on h7
patterns.detect: bishop or knight captures on h7/h2
openings: Scotch and other open centres, where your bishop reaches d3 and the centre is already resolved.
preconditions: A bishop bearing on h7 along the b1-h7 diagonal.
A knight able to reach g5 in one move, with the queen able to follow to h5.
No defending knight on f6, and no ...g6 resource that meets the check safely.
Their pieces far from the kingside — a rook on f8 and a bishop on e7 are not defenders, they are spectators.
patterns.mechanism: Bxh7+ drags the king to h7, Ng5+ arrives with check so there is no time to consolidate, and Qh5 brings the third attacker before the king can run. The whole thing is a forcing sequence — if any move in it is not check, count again.
patterns.defence: Keep a knight on f6 and the h-pawn where it is. If the bishop reaches d3 and your knight has left f6, the sacrifice is on the board whether or not they see it, so treat ...Nf6 as a defensive duty and not just a developing move.

patterns.name: The sacrifice on g7
openings: Modern and Grünfeld — g7 is the square your fianchettoed bishop stands on, and the square that becomes a hole the moment it leaves.
preconditions: The fianchettoed bishop is gone or can be traded off.
A queen that can reach h6 or g7, usually via d2 after Bh6.
The dark squares round the king unguarded — no knight on f6 covering h7 and h5.
Heavy pieces able to join down the g- or h-file.
patterns.mechanism: Trade the g7-bishop first, usually with Bh6. Once it is gone the dark squares round the king belong to whoever puts a piece there, and the sacrifice on g7 is the way to open the last door.
patterns.defence: Do not trade the g7-bishop for free. If Bh6 comes, taking is often right but then the knight must come to f6 and the king to h8 with a rook to g8. In the Modern this is exactly what the 150 Attack is trying to do to you, which is why the tab there tells you to race on the queenside rather than defend passively.

patterns.name: The knight lands next to the king
patterns.detect: a knight moves to f5/f4/h5/h4 beside the enemy king
openings: Modern, Grünfeld and the Scotch alike — the square is f5 against a kingside fianchetto and f4 or h5 against a normal castled position.
preconditions: The landing square cannot be met by a pawn, or the piece is worth more than the pawn that takes it.
Taking the knight opens a line you want open — gxf5 shatters the fianchetto and hands you the long diagonal.
Enough force already aimed at the king that the open line is worth a piece.
patterns.mechanism: The knight is not really going to f5 to be taken: it is going there so that the pawn in front of the king has to decide. Take it and the structure breaks; leave it and the knight hits g7, e7 and h6 forever.
patterns.defence: Count what the open line is worth before capturing. Very often declining is right and the knight, for all its menace, achieves nothing on its own.

patterns.name: The queen gets to h6 or h5
patterns.detect: the queen moves into the ring of squares round the king
openings: Every opening on this page. In the Modern and Grünfeld it arrives via Qd2 and Bh6; in the Scotch it comes to h5 the moment the f- or h-file opens.
preconditions: A second attacker already there or one move away — a queen alone next to a king is a loose queen.
An escape square covered, or a mate on the square she lands on.
No defender able to come to f6, g6 or h6 with tempo.
patterns.mechanism: The queen is the piece that delivers mate and almost never the piece that creates the threat. The order is always the same: open a line, put a minor piece or a rook on it, and only then bring her.
patterns.defence: Watch the square she is heading for, not the square she is on. If h6 or h5 is covered twice and your knight can reach f6 or f8, the attack has nothing.

patterns.name: The h-file battering ram
patterns.detect: a pawn or rook opens and uses the h-file
openings: Modern against the 150 Attack, and the Grünfeld whenever White castles long and your king is behind ...g6.
preconditions: Opposite-side castling, or a White king that is not going to be bothered by the pawn leaving.
A target: the g6-pawn, which after h4-h5 must either take or be taken.
A rook already on h1, so the file opens onto something.
patterns.mechanism: h4-h5 and the g6-pawn has no good answer. Taking opens the h-file; declining lets hxg6 open it anyway. The attack costs no pieces, which is what makes it so common at club level.
patterns.defence: Meet h4 with ...h5. It costs a tempo and ends the plan — without h4-h5 there is no ram, and White has to find a slow idea instead. This is the single most useful defensive move in the whole Modern repertoire.

patterns.name: The forced mate
openings: Wherever the attack has already arrived — these are the positions the other patterns are trying to reach.
preconditions: The king has no flight square, or every flight square is covered.
A forcing move exists — a check, or a capture that cannot be declined.
The defenders cannot interpose with tempo.
patterns.mechanism: By this stage calculation replaces judgement. Check every check, including the ones that hang a piece, because a sacrifice that removes the last defender is exactly what a mating net is made of.
patterns.defence: The time to defend was three moves ago. If you are reading this in a real game, look for a counter-check or a piece you can give back to buy the king a square.

patterns.name: Traps from your games
patterns.detect: opening landmines you fell into — and ones you could have sprung
preconditions: You have reached a known Scotch or Modern shape from your repertoire.
A quiet pawn move or a check looks tempting but leaves a piece or the king hanging.
Or the opponent has just left a piece loose under one of yours.
patterns.mechanism: Stop before the flashy check or the quiet pawn. Ask what hangs after your move, and what hangs on theirs. The drill is two or three forcing moves — the same length as a real trap.
patterns.defence: If you are the one who fell in, the defence is not to play the lemon. Find the alternative that keeps the king safe or the piece guarded, then play the short punishing line so the pattern sticks.

puzzles.note: f3 walks into ...dxc3+. Bh4 (or Re1) keeps the attack without opening the king.
...Nc4+ hangs the knight to Bxc4. Put the rook on the e-file first.
...Nf6 walks into Nxc6. Slide the bishop to b6 first.
Bb5+ wins more cleanly than Bxf7+.
The c6-knight is loose under your d4-knight. Take it.
puzzles.trap_name: Take the loose knight on c6
